short: The first mass tank attack, which broke the Hindenburg Line and could not hold it.
full:
On 20 November 1917 Byng's Third Army attacked on dry chalk downland south-west of Cambrai with 476 tanks, 378 of them fighting machines, and no preliminary bombardment. The guns had been ranged by survey and sound-ranging rather than by firing, so surprise was complete. Tanks carried fascines of brushwood to drop into the Hindenburg Line's wide trenches, and worked in threes with the infantry. The line was pierced to a depth of five miles in a day, ground that had cost months elsewhere, and church bells were rung in England.

By nightfall 179 tanks were out of action, many broken down or ditched rather than hit, and at Flesquières a stubborn defence by German field guns firing over open sights showed what artillery could do to a tank in the open. There were no reserves to exploit the breach. On 30 November the Germans counter-attacked with infiltrating storm troops and took back most of the gains. Cambrai settled nothing on the ground, but it established how tanks, guns and infantry should be used together.
